transcript:
Meeting header: 2027-07-14 16:00 PDT | Duration 52m | Attendees: Priya, Jonah, Leah (Redwood); Maya, Samuel, Renee, Ibrahim (AstraNova)

Summary: quick agenda run, parity-first demo, deep dive on three representative prompts, action items and POC schedule.

00:00 Priya (Redwood AE): hey everyone, thanks for joining, i'm Priya from Redwood Inference, alex couldn't make it today so i'm covering AE side and Jonah will own the technical mapping. how are you folks doing?
00:06 Maya (AstraNova CTO): good, thanks. caffeinated. we have about 50 minutes, want to get through the mapping and then q&a.
00:12 Jonah (Redwood SE): great — i'll start with a quick note: we built the parity sheet to be explicit about tokenization, request/response fields, streaming and function call mapping. it's not magic but it's a deterministic translation.
00:24 Samuel (AstraNova): that sounds good. our main worry is subtle differences in tokenization and temperature semantics — we've seen drift when moving models.
00:32 Jonah: yeah, totally. so first slide, tokenization: OpenAI and Together share similar bpe variants but Anthropic's tokenizer sometimes splits certain long-chemical names differently which impacts stop sequence matching. Redwood uses a tokenizer that can be set to match the source at request time, and our SDK has a shim that normalizes token counts for billing parity.
00:51 Renee (Product): wait, when you say shim, do you mean we have to modify code paths in prod?
01:00 Jonah: minimal. typically it's one line in the client adapter — we include a small normalization helper. examples in the parity spreadsheet.
01:08 Maya: ok, show us an example with a real prompt from our QA flow — the drug-interaction check sample we sent.
01:14 Jonah: sure, pull up prompt A... (typing) so on OpenAI you call /v1/completions with model gpt-x, temperature .2, stop tokens set — on Redwood API the equivalent is a POST to /v1/generate with model name redwood-x, param map: temperature -> temperature, top_p -> top_p. for stop sequences we support both array and newline delimited strings, we map and preserve semantics. here's a note: Anthropic has a slightly different "eos" semantics, we add a small post-filter to align output length in the parity layer.
01:44 Maya: that post-filter concerns me for latency — is it expensive?
01:49 Jonah: negligible at p50, maybe a 1-2ms extra CPU pass; at p99 it can add up if you have millions of calls, which is why we recommend application-level stop heuristics where possible.
02:03 Ibrahim (DevOps): what's the plan for streaming? we rely on streaming for progressive UI updates.
02:08 Jonah: Redwood supports chunked streaming compatible with EventStream over HTTP and gRPC streams for our SDKs. streaming chunk size defaults are smaller but tunable. we also have a compatibility mode that emulates OpenAI chunk boundaries to minimize client changes.
02:26 Samuel: about function calling: Together's schema has nested objects, we use them for structured extraction. can Redwood map Together's function_call exactly?
02:34 Jonah: function tooling mapping: yes, the mapping is 1:1 for basic cases — name, args, and call patterns. for deeply nested combined schemas there's some normalization required; we'll show the mapping in the spreadsheet. for calls that require synchronous external lookup we recommend using Redwood's tool-calling integration which can handle retries, auth headers, and ephemeral prober hooks.
02:56 Priya: short commercial interjection — Dedicated nodes give you consistent p99 latency and isolation for PHI workflows; Private deployment adds VPC and KMS hooks for key control.
03:09 Maya: what's needed for KMS? we use HashiCorp Vault in KMS mode and AWS KMS for staging.
03:15 Jonah: two options: for Private you can either bring-your-own-HSM via our on-prem bundle (we integrate with PKCS11 and common HSMs) or in VPC you can configure Redwood to use your AWS KMS with customer-managed keys. we'll include the config example in the security pack.
03:32 Renee: curious about token billing parity. we bill by token on OpenAI — how do we avoid surprises?
03:37 Priya: Redwood's billing exposes tokenization counts per request, and the parity shim tags requests with original model source so you get apples-to-apples comparisons. we'll include a cost-comparison row in the spreadsheet with estimated per-1M tokens for your traffic profile.
03:52 Samuel: benching — we want p50/p95/p99 latencies and output-determinism checks across the three vendors. can Redwood run a bench or do we run it?
04:01 Jonah: we can run it in partnership. simplest: you give us sample prompts and a traffic profile, we run bench on hosted and dedicated presets and return CSVs + artifacts. for private deployments we'll ship a bench harness you can run locally.
04:18 Maya: awesome. show us the parity spreadsheet now if you can.
04:21 Jonah: pulling up screen — spreadsheet has tabs: tokens, params, streaming, function_calls, edge-cases. token tab shows a column "expected delta" which flags where Anthropic tokenization is +1 token often for hyphenated chemical names. param tab maps OpenAI's "max_tokens" -> Redwood's "max_new_tokens" and Together's response trimming behavior is noted.
04:45 Maya: any gotchas for our current retry logic? we use exponential backoff with jitter right now.
04:50 Jonah: Redwood's SDK returns standard HTTP 429 and an idempotency token for retries. note: when using streaming + retries there's a window where partial chunks could be double-processed if your client doesn't handle idempotency; our SDK includes helpers to reconcile.
05:10 Ibrahim: network topology: for VPC Private what's the path? do you push a connector or do we pull?
05:16 Jonah: in VPC mode we deploy a customer-managed control plane; traffic for inference can either route via a private peering connection to Redwood's serving region or you can host inference entirely on-prem with our appliance. for peering it's a direct ENI or interconnect and we do not route through public internet. we'll give a network diagram in the docs.
05:36 Priya: quick pause — any specific compliance questions? SOC2, HIPAA, EU data residency?
05:41 Maya: HIPAA is a must for the clinical notes pipeline. EU residency less urgent but good to know.
05:46 Priya: we have HIPAA attestation options on Private and Dedicated with BAA; hosted customers can get contract addendum for enterprise tiers. we'll put that text in the security pack.
05:58 Jonah: demo: i'm going to show a quick cURL mapping from OpenAI-style to Redwood. (typing) Example 1: completions with stop sequences -> Redwood /v1/generate. show mapping: max_tokens -> max_new_tokens; echo -> stream false/true preserved. here's the sample output — notice how we preserve stop tokens.
06:32 Renee: does Redwood's generator default to greedy or sampling?
06:35 Jonah: sampling by default with temperature 1.0; we preserve temperature semantics but note that certain quantized variants slightly change distribution, we document recommended temperature adjustments in the spreadsheet.
06:50 Samuel: quantization — we plan to use q4 and q5 models in Dedicated. how does that affect hallucination or temperature scaling?
06:57 Jonah: quantization mostly affects likelihood calibration; small offsets can be fixed with prompt tuning or small temperature tweaks. we've observed a 0.05-0.1 temperature effective shift in some dense generation tasks; we'll include model-specific guidance.
07:16 Maya: okay, show me the streaming compatibility mode.
07:21 Jonah: enabling compatibility_mode=true returns chunk boundaries that match OpenAI eventstream deltas. we'll show the header differences; it's purely a runtime toggle.
07:34 Maya: any risk to throughput when enabling compatibility mode?
07:37 Jonah: negligible p50; maybe 3-5% throughput decrease under high qps because of smaller chunking and more flushes.
07:47 Priya: if throughput is a concern, autoscaling Dedicated pools can be tuned to favor larger batching windows; Optimize can recommend batching parameters based on your real traffic.
07:59 Renee: what's Optimize? we've seen references but not used it.
08:03 Priya: Redwood Optimize is our recommendations engine — it analyzes request distributions and suggests batching window sizes, cache prefixes, and quantization tiers to minimize cost while hitting latency SLOs. we can run it against your traffic in the POC.
08:20 Samuel: for the POC we need reproducible outputs for regression testing. what's the reproducibility story?
08:26 Jonah: we support deterministic seeds for sampling on supported models; for quantized or distilled models we provide a "regression mode" that pins kernels and disables non-deterministic op reorderings. that'll be part of the bench harness.
08:42 Maya: question about caching — we have a lot of repeated prefixes in clinical notes, could prefix caching cause privacy issues?
08:48 Jonah: prefix caching stores KV caches in memory on the serving node; for hosted we encrypt in transit and at rest and caches are ephemeral per-request lifetime. for Private/Dedicated you can opt to disable prefix caching or enable per-tenant isolated caches. we'll document default TTLs and eviction.
09:05 Ibrahim: and logs — we need audit trail for every tokenized request for e-discovery. what's available?
09:11 Leah (CSM): Redwood Console exposes per-token traces and full request/response unless suppressed; audit logs can be exported to your SIEM via S3 or pushed to a logging endpoint. access is RBAC controlled.
09:26 Maya: let's talk about the POC plan — we need to validate output equivalence within an acceptable threshold and measure latency and cost.
09:33 Priya: typical POC: we run A/B against your OpenAI/Together/Anthropic baseline with a 3k-10k sample set, measure BLEU/ROUGE-ish metrics you care about and p50/p95/p99 latencies, then we produce a regression report and optimization recommendations.
09:51 Samuel: timeline? can this start next week if we get the prompts ready?
09:55 Priya: yes, if we get prompts and traffic profile this week we can start benching mid-next-week and have results in 5 business days.
10:03 Maya: show cost-estimate now? not a detailed quote but rough per-1M tokens for hosted + dedicated.
10:09 Priya: hosted starter numbers: redwood-hosted standard model ~ $X per 1M tokens, dedicated depends on instance type — Leah will produce a sample quote in next steps.
10:20 Leah: I'll produce three scenarios in the quote: hosted, small dedicated pool (for predictable latency), and private appliance.
10:27 Renee: on function calling, do you support call-backs and tool auth natively? for example, a function that calls our internal drug DB needs to present a short-lived JWT.
10:36 Jonah: yes — tool calling supports ephemeral auth tokens and pluggable retrievers. we have a pattern called "tool bridge" where the runtime invokes your endpoint with signed short-lived headers. we can also run a proxy in VPC to terminate inside your network.
10:52 Ibrahim: curious: what's the rollback story if we see a regression in quality after switching?
10:57 Priya: rollbacks are standard: you can pin to previous model version or fallback to a vendor adapter; Redwood supports per-route fallback policies so you could route critical flows back to your previous provider while you fix parity.
11:14 Maya: are there customer stories for regulated workloads?
11:18 Priya: yes — a few anonymized case studies: one medtech, one fintech; i'll share them in the security pack.
11:25 Samuel: okay, last technical ask — can we tweak the KV cache TTL per-route?
11:29 Jonah: yes, per-route TTL and per-tenant isolation both supported in Dedicated/Private.
11:36 Priya: wrapping up, recap of next steps and who's doing what.
11:40 Maya: sounds good.
11:42 Priya: action items as discussed: parity spreadsheet, security pack, sample bench run. Jonah and Leah will coordinate the technical artifacts, i'll follow up on commercial.
11:53 Renee: thanks everyone.
11:55 Meeting end.

Notes on transcription: filler words kept, occasional mis-heard acronyms (we saw "eos" flagged as "E O S" in a couple places), speaker overlaps minimal.
